title: Design an In-Memory Key-Value Store / Cache — Object Model
prompt: Design the object model for an in-memory key-value store / cache (like a simplified Redis or Guava Cache). It supports get and put, per-entry TTL expiration, a bounded capacity with a pluggable eviction policy (LRU, LFU, FIFO), and must be thread-safe. Design the core classes, the eviction-policy abstraction, the TTL mechanism, and the concurrency approach. Sketch the class diagram.
blurb: Bounded cache with pluggable eviction (LRU/LFU/FIFO) via Strategy, TTL expiry, and a real thread-safety story.

rubric.label: Requirements clarification
rubric.description: Separates functional (get/put/delete, TTL, bounded capacity, eviction) from non-functional (O(1) ops, thread-safety, pluggable policy).

rubric.label: Core entities
rubric.description: Cache, Entry (value+metadata), EvictionPolicy, TTL/Clock, Store/backing map — cleanly separated.

rubric.label: Class design & responsibilities
rubric.description: Eviction policy is decoupled from the store; Entry carries expiry + access metadata; Cache coordinates.

rubric.label: Relationships & cardinality
rubric.description: Cache has one Store and one EvictionPolicy; Store maps key→Entry; policy tracks ordering over keys. Composition reasoned.

rubric.label: Design patterns
rubric.description: Strategy for eviction policy, optional Observer/callbacks for eviction/expiry notifications, Factory for policy creation, Decorator for stats/loading cache.

rubric.label: SOLID / OCP
rubric.description: Adding a new eviction policy plugs in without touching Cache; TTL and eviction concerns separated (SRP).

rubric.label: API / method design
rubric.description: get(k), put(k,v,ttl), delete(k), size, and policy hooks onAccess/onInsert/evictCandidate — clear signatures.

rubric.label: Concurrency & performance
rubric.description: Thread-safe get/put with good throughput; O(1) LRU via hashmap+doubly-linked-list; lock granularity/striping. THE core challenge.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Expired-but-not-evicted lazy vs active expiry, capacity 1, update existing key, evict vs expire ordering, negative TTL.

rubric.label: Extensibility
rubric.description: New policies, size-based (weight) eviction, write-through/read-through loader, stats, persistence added cleanly.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Narrates the data-structure choice and locking strategy, states tradeoffs, reasons about O(1) LRU.

functional_requirements: get(key) → value or miss; put(key, value) with optional TTL; delete(key)
Bounded maximum size; when full, evict per the configured policy
Pluggable eviction policy: LRU, LFU, FIFO (extensible)
Per-entry TTL: expired entries are not returned and are reclaimed
Thread-safe concurrent access from many threads
nonfunctional_requirements: Thread-safe with good concurrent throughput (not one global lock if avoidable)
Eviction policy swappable without editing the cache core (OCP)
TTL and eviction are independent concerns
clarifying_questions: Which eviction policies must we support at launch — LRU, LFU, FIFO?
Is the bound a count of entries or a total size/weight (bytes)?
TTL expiry — lazy (on access), active (background sweeper), or both?
Read-through/write-through loader, or a plain cache the app fills?
Expected concurrency level — do we need lock striping / a concurrent map?
Do we need eviction/expiry notifications or stats?

core_classes.name: Cache<K,V>
core_classes.responsibility: Facade coordinating store, eviction policy, and TTL; exposes get/put/delete.

core_classes.name: CacheEntry<V>
core_classes.responsibility: Wraps a value with metadata for TTL and eviction bookkeeping.

core_classes.name: EvictionPolicy<K> (abstract)
core_classes.responsibility: Strategy: tracks usage order and names the next eviction candidate.

core_classes.name: LruPolicy
core_classes.responsibility: Recency order via HashMap + doubly-linked list; evicts the tail (LRU) in O(1).

core_classes.name: LfuPolicy
core_classes.responsibility: Frequency buckets; evicts the least-frequently-used (ties broken by recency).

core_classes.name: FifoPolicy
core_classes.responsibility: Insertion-order queue; evicts the oldest inserted.

core_classes.name: ExpirationManager
core_classes.responsibility: Handles TTL: lazy check on access and/or an active background sweeper.

relationships: Cache composes one Store, one EvictionPolicy, one Clock, and optionally an ExpirationManager and RemovalListener.
Store maps key → CacheEntry; CacheEntry holds the value + TTL/eviction metadata.
EvictionPolicy tracks an ordering over keys and is notified by the Cache on every access/insert/remove.
The LRU implementation itself is a HashMap + doubly-linked list giving O(1) reorder and evict.
EvictionPolicyFactory decouples Cache from concrete policy classes (DIP).

design_patterns.why: Eviction algorithm varies independently; new policies plug in without editing Cache (OCP).
Constructs the configured policy and decouples Cache from concretes.
Decouples side effects (metrics, write-back) from cache mutation.

design_patterns.where: StatsCache / LoadingCache wrapping the base Cache
design_patterns.why: Adds hit/miss stats or read-through loading without changing the core cache.

apis: V get(K key)  // returns null/miss if absent or expired; updates policy
void put(K key, V value, Duration ttl)  // evicts if over capacity
policy hooks: onAccess(K), onInsert(K), onRemove(K), evictCandidate() -> K
state_transitions: Entry: ABSENT → LIVE (put) → LIVE (get bumps recency/frequency) → EXPIRED (now > expiryAt) → REMOVED (lazy on access or active sweep)
On put when at capacity: policy.evictCandidate() → remove that key → then insert new
get on an expired entry: treat as miss, remove, fire RemovalListener(EXPIRED)
put on an existing key: update value + policy.onAccess, no capacity change
edge_cases: Expired but not yet swept → get must treat it as a miss and reclaim it (lazy expiry)
Capacity of 1 → put evicts the single existing entry
put on an existing key must update in place, not double-count size
Simultaneous expiry and eviction of the same key → idempotent removal
Negative/zero TTL → never store or immediately expire, define explicitly
LFU tie-break among equal-frequency keys → fall back to recency/FIFO
Hot miss stampede when many threads miss the same key (with a loader) → single-flight
concurrency: Simplest: one lock around get/put — correct but a throughput bottleneck
Better: lock striping / segmented map (like ConcurrentHashMap) so operations on different keys don't contend
The LRU doubly-linked list is the tricky shared structure — every get mutates it; guard it or use per-segment LRU or an approximate LRU (sampling / second-chance) to reduce contention
Active TTL sweeper runs on a background thread; removals must be atomic with reads
RemovalListener callbacks fired outside the lock to avoid deadlock/latency
extensibility: New policy (MRU, TinyLFU, segmented-LRU) → new Strategy, register in factory
Weight/size-based bound → policy evicts until total weight fits, entries carry a weight
Read-through/write-through → LoadingCache decorator with a loader function
Persistence/snapshotting → an optional writer, orthogonal to the core

deep_dives.probe: How do you make LRU get and evict both O(1)? Walk me through the HashMap + doubly-linked-list and exactly what happens on a get.
Show the EvictionPolicy interface and how the Cache stays unaware of whether it's LRU, LFU, or FIFO. Add LFU — what's the data structure and the tie-break rule?
Lazy vs active expiration — what are the tradeoffs? If you use a background sweeper, what structure orders entries by expiry, and how does it coexist with lazy checks on read?
A single global lock kills throughput. How do you reduce contention while keeping the LRU list consistent — striping, per-segment LRU, or approximate LRU? Defend the tradeoff.
Every get must notify the policy to update recency/frequency. How do you keep that hook clean without leaking policy internals into the Store?

followup_bank.question: Make both get and evict O(1) for LRU. What two data structures do you combine, and what happens on a cache hit?
Swap LRU for LFU. How much of Cache changes? If any, your policy isn't properly decoupled.

followup_bank.trigger: mentions ttl or expire or expiry
followup_bank.question: Lazy or active expiration? If active, what orders entries by expiry time and how does it coexist with lazy checks?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions lock or synchronized or thread
followup_bank.question: A single global lock serializes every get. How do you get concurrency while keeping the LRU list correct?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions concurrenthashmap or segment or stripe
followup_bank.question: With striping, how do you maintain a globally-correct LRU order, or do you settle for approximate LRU? What do you lose?

tradeoffs: Global lock (simple, correct, low throughput) vs lock striping (high throughput, weaker global ordering)
Exact LRU (precise, contended list) vs approximate LRU / sampling (cheap, slightly worse hit rate)
Lazy TTL (no background thread, stale memory held) vs active sweeper (prompt reclaim, extra thread + structure)
Count-based capacity (simple) vs weight-based (accurate memory bound, more bookkeeping)
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer separates three concerns: a Store (key→CacheEntry map), an EvictionPolicy Strategy (LRU/LFU/FIFO created by a factory), and TTL handling — and keeps Cache as the coordinator that notifies the policy on every access/insert. It nails O(1) LRU via a HashMap plus a doubly-linked list (get moves the node to the head, evict removes the tail) and gives LFU frequency buckets with a recency tie-break. For TTL it combines lazy expiry on read with an optional background sweeper ordered by expiry time. The concurrency answer is the differentiator: acknowledge that a global lock throttles throughput and propose lock striping / per-segment LRU or an approximate (sampling/second-chance) LRU, honestly stating the exact-ordering tradeoff. Adding a new policy touches zero Cache code (OCP).

interviewer_notes: Let them state which policies and TTL mode to support. Two make-or-break areas: (1) O(1) LRU via hashmap + doubly-linked list — make them walk a get step by step; and (2) thread-safety beyond a single global lock. Most candidates reach for 'synchronize everything'; push them toward striping / per-segment or approximate LRU and get them to name what correctness they give up. Verify EvictionPolicy is a clean Strategy (test with 'swap to LFU'). Probe lazy vs active TTL and how the two coexist. Keep it object-design and data-structure focused, not a distributed-Redis discussion.
